projects.title: Solution to Meet the Air Force Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Scheduling — Phase II
projects.sponsor: U.S. Department of Defense / U.S. Department of the Air Force
projects.detail: Optimization and AI-based decision support for strategic planning of humanitarian logistics operations.
projects.context: I contributed to a decision support system for planning humanitarian relief operations. The project combined mathematical optimization with a priority-based heuristic to select participating organizations, allocate supplies, and choose transport modes and delivery speeds. The model accounts for delivery priorities, available resources, and the costs of supplies, delays, fuel and crews.

projects.title: Selection of Level Crossings for Closure in the State of Florida: An Optimization-based Approach
projects.detail: Decision support for level-crossing closure selection, combining highway safety with freight-flow considerations.
projects.context: I contributed to a decision support system for selecting highway–rail crossings for closure in Florida. The model weighs safety, economic and environmental benefits subject to budget and closure eligibility constraints. A selection heuristic and an interactive interface support comparisons of alternative closure strategies.

researchStatement: Operations research and AI for maritime transportation, logistics and supply chains.
biography: My research combines operations research, mathematical optimization and artificial intelligence to study planning and decision-making in maritime transportation, logistics and supply chains. I investigate how interdependent decisions about capacity, schedules and resource allocation affect operating performance, and how these decisions should adapt to uncertainty and disruption.

I am a Postdoctoral Scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus. I earned my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering at Florida State University in August 2025, advised by Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets, and remained there as a Postdoctoral Research Scholar until May 2026. I also hold a Master of Engineering in Civil Engineering from Florida State University and a Bachelor of Science in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University.
homeResearch: My research addresses the coordination of decisions within facilities and across supply chains. Published studies examine berth allocation and vessel scheduling, freight transfers at cross-docking terminals, and liner-shipping schedule recovery. These settings motivate broader questions about how production, inventory and transportation should be coordinated, how operating flexibility changes the value of capacity, and how organizations reconcile conflicting objectives.

I develop mathematical formulations, decomposition approaches and learning-guided search algorithms. My berth-scheduling and cross-docking research combines compact mixed-integer models with adaptive computation and exact optimization. My longer-term interests include reinforcement learning for sequential decisions and generative AI for representing operating requirements, developing formulations and coordinating decisions across multiple agents.

I am also interested in supply chain resilience, automation and electrification, and healthcare and humanitarian operations. Across these areas, I study the relationship between decisions made in advance and the operating options available afterward. Questions include how to position reserve resources, when to revise existing commitments, and how supporting infrastructure affects the performance of new technologies.
academicContext: I earned my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from Florida State University in August 2025 under the supervision of Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets. Florida State University also awarded me a Master of Engineering in Civil Engineering in December 2024 during my doctoral studies. I received my Bachelor of Science in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University in June 2022.

My doctoral dissertation, “Effective Hyperheuristic Algorithms for the Berth Scheduling Problem at Marine Container Terminals,” examined adaptive algorithm selection for terminal scheduling. Subsequent research has developed compact formulations, decomposition approaches and hybrid search methods for berth scheduling and cross-docking. Collaborative work addresses liner-shipping recovery, pharmaceutical supply chains, electric-vehicle scheduling and transportation infrastructure investment.

After serving as a Postdoctoral Research Scholar at Florida State University from August 2025 to May 2026, I joined the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus in June 2026. I work with Dr. Angela Kitali on transportation research and proposal development involving computer vision, infrastructure inventories and geospatial analysis. My broader research program concerns optimization and AI for logistics, industrial and service systems.

homeQuestions: When should production, inventory and transportation decisions be coordinated, and how should the benefits and risks of coordination be shared?
How should capacity, inventory and operating flexibility be positioned before disruptions and redeployed during recovery?
How can learning and generative AI improve mathematical modeling and sequential decisions while preserving feasibility and operational priorities?

collaborationProfiles.title: Mathematical optimization and logistics
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets and collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My doctoral and postdoctoral research with Dr. Maxim A. Dulebenets developed formulations and algorithms for berth scheduling and cross-docking. This collaboration examines how compact models, decomposition and adaptive search can exploit operational structure, with published studies addressing both the design of solution methods and their computational performance.

collaborationProfiles.title: Port electrification and transportation infrastructure
collaborationProfiles.people: Dr. Angela Kitali, Soud Mbegele and project collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My published work with Soud Mbegele and Dr. Angela Kitali examines how the Northwest Seaport Alliance translated shore power commitments into implementation responsibilities. I also contribute to research planning on computer vision and geospatial analysis for transportation facility inventories.
collaborationProfiles.label: Shore power commitments and implementation accountability

collaborationProfiles.title: Safety and resource allocation
collaborationProfiles.people: Ren Moses, Eren E. Ozguven, John Sobanjo and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Our highway–rail crossing publications connect mathematical optimization with safety and infrastructure planning. The work ranges from closure selection to multi-objective allocation among closures, countermeasures and grade separation. A collaborative review examines how these approaches represent costs, collision risk, sustainability and community considerations. The publications identify the specific author teams and study designs.
collaborationProfiles.label: Rail-crossing decision study

collaborationProfiles.title: Adaptive algorithms and sustainable systems
collaborationProfiles.people: Marta Borowska-Stefańska, Szymon Wiśniewski, Yui-Yip Lau and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: These collaborations include berth-scheduling reviews, adaptive cross-docking algorithms, ship-schedule recovery and studies of electric-vehicle and tugboat operations. They combine mathematical modeling with different forms of evidence, including computational comparison, literature synthesis and industry interviews. The common methodological interest is how operating constraints and competing objectives should shape the model and its solution procedure.
collaborationProfiles.label: Joint publications and full author lists
